blocks.prompt: 7 (a) Convert each of the following equation into (i) Slope-intercept form (ii) Two-point form (iii) Intercept form (iv) Point-slope form (v) Normal form (vi) Symmetric form: \(2x + 3y - 6 = 0\)
blocks.explanation:
One line, six ways of writing it. The line does not change; only its form does.
Each form shows a different feature: slope, two points, intercepts, a point and the slope, the perpendicular from the origin, the inclination.
Plan: slope and intercepts first, then build each form from them.
steps:
Given: \(2x + 3y - 6 = 0\).
To find: the six standard forms (i)-(vi).
Method: as in Example 6. Get \(y\) alone for the slope; take the two intercept points \((x\text{-intercept}, 0)\) and \((0, y\text{-intercept})\) for the two-point and point-slope forms; divide by \(\pm\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}\) for the normal form; take \(\sin\theta\), \(\cos\theta\) from \(\tan\theta = m\) for the symmetric form.

(i) Slope-intercept form
\[3y = -2x + 6\]
\[y = -\dfrac{2}{3}x + 2\]
Why: make \(y\) the subject; slope \(m = -\frac{2}{3}\), \(y\)-intercept \(c = 2\).

Two points on the line
Put \(y = 0\): \(x = 3\); put \(x = 0\): \(y = 2\). Points \((3, 0)\) and \((0, 2)\).
Why: the intercept points are the easiest points to find (the book uses them too).

(iii) Intercept form
\[2x + 3y = 6\]
\[\dfrac{2x}{6} + \dfrac{3y}{6} = 1\]
\[\dfrac{x}{3} + \dfrac{y}{2} = 1\]
Why: move the constant to the right and divide by it, so the right side is 1; the denominators are the intercepts \(a = 3\), \(b = 2\).

(iv) Point-slope form
\[y - 0 = -\dfrac{2}{3}(x - 3)\]
Why: \(y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)\) with the point \((3, 0)\) and \(m = -\frac{2}{3}\).

(v) Normal form
\[\sqrt{2^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{13}\]
\[\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{13}}x + \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}}y = \dfrac{6}{\sqrt{13}}\]
Why: write it as \(ax + by = -c\) and divide by \(+\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}\) so that the right side \(p\) is positive. Here \(-c\) is already positive, so the sign is \(+\). Then \(x\cos\alpha + y\sin\alpha = p\) with \(\cos\alpha = \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}, \sin\alpha = \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}, p = \frac{6}{\sqrt{13}}\) (\(\alpha \approx 56.31^\circ\)).

(vi) Symmetric form
\[\tan\theta = -\dfrac{2}{3}\]
\[\sin\theta = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\]
\[\cos\theta = -\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\]
\[\dfrac{x - 3}{-\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}} = \dfrac{y - 0}{\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}} = r\]
Why: \(\theta\) is the inclination, \(0^\circ \le \theta < 180^\circ\), so \(\sin\theta \ge 0\). \(\tan\theta < 0\) means \(\theta\) is obtuse, so \(\cos\theta < 0\). Then \(\frac{x - x_1}{\cos\theta} = \frac{y - y_1}{\sin\theta} = r\) with the point \((3, 0)\).

Check:
Cross-multiplying the symmetric form:
\[\tfrac{2}{\sqrt{13}}(x - 3) = -\tfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}}y\]
\[2x + 3y - 6 = 0\]
which is the given equation. Every form can be checked the same way by expanding it back. (The book prints no answers for this question; forms that use other points are also correct if they expand to the same line.)

blocks.prompt: 7 (b) Convert each of the following equation into (i) Slope-intercept form (ii) Two-point form (iii) Intercept form (iv) Point-slope form (v) Normal form (vi) Symmetric form: \(x - 2y + 4 = 0\)
blocks.explanation:
One line, six ways of writing it. The line does not change; only its form does.
Each form shows a different feature: slope, two points, intercepts, a point and the slope, the perpendicular from the origin, the inclination.
Plan: slope and intercepts first, then build each form from them.
steps:
Given: \(x - 2y + 4 = 0\).
To find: the six standard forms (i)-(vi).
Method: as in Example 6. Get \(y\) alone for the slope; take the two intercept points \((x\text{-intercept}, 0)\) and \((0, y\text{-intercept})\) for the two-point and point-slope forms; divide by \(\pm\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}\) for the normal form; take \(\sin\theta\), \(\cos\theta\) from \(\tan\theta = m\) for the symmetric form.

(i) Slope-intercept form
\[2y = x + 4\]
\[y = \dfrac{1}{2}x + 2\]
Why: make \(y\) the subject; slope \(m = \frac{1}{2}\), \(y\)-intercept \(c = 2\).

Two points on the line
Put \(y = 0\): \(x = -4\); put \(x = 0\): \(y = 2\). Points \((-4, 0)\) and \((0, 2)\).
Why: the intercept points are the easiest points to find (the book uses them too).

(iii) Intercept form
\[x - 2y = -4\]
\[\dfrac{x}{-4} + \dfrac{-2y}{-4} = 1\]
\[\dfrac{x}{-4} + \dfrac{y}{2} = 1\]
Why: move the constant to the right and divide by it, so the right side is 1; the denominators are the intercepts \(a = -4\), \(b = 2\).

(iv) Point-slope form
\[y - 0 = \dfrac{1}{2}(x + 4)\]
Why: \(y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)\) with the point \((-4, 0)\) and \(m = \frac{1}{2}\).

(v) Normal form
\[\sqrt{1^2 + (-2)^2} = \sqrt{5}\]
\[-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}x + \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}y = \dfrac{4}{\sqrt{5}}\]
Why: write it as \(ax + by = -c\) and divide by \(-\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}\) so that the right side \(p\) is positive. Here \(-c = -4\) is negative, so we divide by the negative root. Then \(x\cos\alpha + y\sin\alpha = p\) with \(\cos\alpha = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}, \sin\alpha = \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}, p = \frac{4}{\sqrt{5}}\) (\(\alpha \approx 116.57^\circ\)).

(vi) Symmetric form
\[\tan\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}\]
\[\sin\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\]
\[\cos\theta = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\]
\[\dfrac{x + 4}{\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}} = \dfrac{y - 0}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}} = r\]
Why: \(\theta\) is the inclination, \(0^\circ \le \theta < 180^\circ\), so \(\sin\theta \ge 0\). \(\tan\theta > 0\) means \(\theta\) is acute, so \(\cos\theta > 0\). Then \(\frac{x - x_1}{\cos\theta} = \frac{y - y_1}{\sin\theta} = r\) with the point \((-4, 0)\).

Check:
Cross-multiplying the symmetric form:
\[\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(x + 4) = \tfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}y\]
\[x - 2y + 4 = 0\]
which is the given equation. Every form can be checked the same way by expanding it back. (The book prints no answers for this question; forms that use other points are also correct if they expand to the same line.)

blocks.prompt: 7 (c) Convert each of the following equation into (i) Slope-intercept form (ii) Two-point form (iii) Intercept form (iv) Point-slope form (v) Normal form (vi) Symmetric form: \(4x + 5y - 20 = 0\)
